pumac-2017-combinatorics-b-01.title: Symmetry (official method)
pumac-2017-combinatorics-b-01.body:
Without restrictions there are $5!=120$ arrangements. Group them by the relative order of M, $\alpha$, C: each of the $3!=6$ relative orders occurs equally often (swapping the three letters' positions maps one group onto another). Exactly one of the $6$ relative orders is M, $\alpha$, C, so the count is $\frac{120}{6}=20$.

**Answer: 20**

pumac-2017-combinatorics-b-01.title: Choose positions
pumac-2017-combinatorics-b-01.body:
Choose which $3$ of the $5$ positions hold M, $\alpha$, C: $\binom53=10$ ways; they must go in that order (one way). Then P and U fill the other two positions in $2$ ways. Total $10\cdot2=20$.

**Answer: 20**

pumac-2017-combinatorics-b-02.title: Burnside's lemma
pumac-2017-combinatorics-b-02.body:
A rotation that makes the tetrahedron "look the same" must send the split face to itself, so only the rotations about the axis through the centre of that face count: the identity and the rotations by $120^\circ$ and $240^\circ$.

- Identity: fixes all $2^7=128$ colorings.
- Each $120^\circ$ rotation: the triangles fall into cycles — the central small triangle (fixed), the three corner small triangles (one 3-cycle), the three other faces (one 3-cycle). A fixed coloring is constant on each cycle: $2^3=8$.

By Burnside, the number of colorings is $\frac{128+8+8}{3}=48$.

**Answer: 48**

pumac-2017-combinatorics-b-02.title: Case count (official method)
pumac-2017-combinatorics-b-02.body:
Color the central small triangle last ($2$ ways; it is fixed by every rotation). For the three corner triangles of the split face:

- **All the same color** (2 ways). Every rotation preserves this, so the other three faces are counted up to rotation: $3$ faces in a $3$-cycle with $2$ colors give $4$ patterns ($0,1,2,3$ orange). That is $2\cdot4=8$.
- **Two of one color, one of the other** (2 ways up to rotation). Now the odd corner triangle pins down the rotation, so the other three faces can be colored freely: $2^3=8$. That is $2\cdot8=16$.

So $8+16=24$ colorings of the six non-central triangles, and $2\cdot24=48$ in total.

**Answer: 48**

pumac-2017-combinatorics-b-03.title: Follow one turtle (official method)
pumac-2017-combinatorics-b-03.body:
Fix one original turtle. When $n$ turtles are present, it is chosen in the next merge with probability $\frac2n$. So it survives all $2015$ merges uncombined with probability
$$\prod_{n=3}^{2017}\left(1-\frac2n\right)=\prod_{n=3}^{2017}\frac{n-2}{n}=\frac{1\cdot2}{2016\cdot2017}.$$
At the end there are two turtles, and at most one of them can be an original that was never combined (otherwise all $2015$ merges happened among the other $2015$ turtles, leaving one super-turtle plus two originals — three turtles, a contradiction). So the events for different turtles are disjoint and the probability is
$$2017\cdot\frac{2}{2016\cdot2017}=\frac{1}{1008}.$$
Hence $p+q=1009$.

**Answer: 1009**

pumac-2017-combinatorics-b-03.title: Check with small cases
pumac-2017-combinatorics-b-03.body:
Repeat the argument for $N$ turtles: the probability is $N\cdot\frac{2}{N(N-1)}=\frac{2}{N-1}$. For $N=3$ this is $1$ (after one merge, the untouched turtle remains) — correct. For $N=4$: after two merges there are two turtles; the second merge is between the super-turtle and an original (prob. $\frac23$, leaving an untouched original) or between the two originals (prob. $\frac13$). So the answer is $\frac23$ — matches. An exact computer calculation for $N=5,6,10,30$ also gives $\frac2{N-1}$. For $N=2017$: $\frac{2}{2016}=\frac1{1008}$.

**Answer: 1009**

pumac-2017-combinatorics-b-04.title: Sum by place value
pumac-2017-combinatorics-b-04.body:
A 3-digit unremarkable number $\overline{abc}$ has $a\in\{1,\dots,9\}$, $b\ne a$, $c\ne b$.

- **Count:** $9\cdot9\cdot9=729$.
- **Hundreds digit:** each $a$ appears with $9\cdot9=81$ choices of $(b,c)$: sum $81\cdot45=3645$.
- **Tens digit:** $b=0$ occurs for all $9$ values of $a$; $b=d\ge1$ occurs for $8$ values of $a$. Each with $9$ choices of $c$. Sum of $b$: $9\cdot8\cdot(1+\dots+9)=3240$.
- **Units digit:** the number of $(a,b)$ with $b\ne c$: for $c=0$, $b\in\{1..9\}$, and for each $b$, $8$ choices of $a$ ($a\ne b$, $a\ne0$) — $72$; for $c=d\ge1$: $b=0$ gives $9$ values of $a$, $b\notin\{0,d\}$ ($8$ values) gives $8$ each, total $9+64=73$. Sum of $c$: $73\cdot45=3285$.

Total: $100\cdot3645+10\cdot3240+3285=364500+32400+3285=400185$.

**Answer: 400185**

pumac-2017-combinatorics-b-04.title: Complement symmetry (official method)
pumac-2017-combinatorics-b-04.body:
Allow leading zeros. Among the $10\cdot9\cdot9=810$ digit strings of length $3$ with no two adjacent digits equal, replacing each digit $d$ by $9-d$ is a bijection that pairs $n$ with $999-n$. So their sum is $810\cdot\frac{999}{2}=404595$.

Remove the strings $0bc$. Their values $10b+c$ are exactly the length-$2$ strings $bc$ with $b\ne0$, $c\ne b$. All $90$ length-$2$ strings with $b\ne c$ sum to $90\cdot\frac{99}{2}=4455$ (same pairing), and those with $b=0$ are $01,\dots,09$, summing to $45$. So the strings $0bc$ sum to $4455-45=4410$.

The answer is $404595-4410=400185$.

**Answer: 400185**

pumac-2017-combinatorics-b-05.title: Bayes (official method)
pumac-2017-combinatorics-b-05.body:
Let $n=100$ and $k$ the number of black balls ($P(k)=\frac{1}{n+1}$). The first ball is black with probability $\frac kn$, so given that it is black, $P(k\mid\text{black})=\frac{k/n}{\sum_j j/n}=\frac{2k}{n(n+1)}$.

Then the second ball is black with probability $\frac{k-1}{n-1}$:
$$P=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{2k}{n(n+1)}\cdot\frac{k-1}{n-1}=\frac{4}{n(n+1)(n-1)}\sum_{k}\binom k2=\frac{4}{(n-1)n(n+1)}\binom{n+1}{3}=\frac23.$$
So $p+q=5$.

**Answer: 5**

pumac-2017-combinatorics-b-05.title: Uniform-mixture trick
pumac-2017-combinatorics-b-05.body:
The colours of the balls in the order they roll out form an exchangeable sequence, and $P(\text{first }j\text{ balls all black})=\frac{1}{j+1}$ (for $j=1$ this is symmetry between the colours; for $j=2$ see the check below). So
$$P(\text{2nd black}\mid\text{1st black})=\frac{P(\text{first two black})}{P(\text{first black})}=\frac{1/3}{1/2}=\frac23.$$
(Check: $P(\text{first two black})=\frac1{101}\sum_k\frac{k(k-1)}{100\cdot99}=\frac{1}{101}\cdot\frac{2\binom{101}3}{9900}=\frac13$.)

**Answer: 5**

pumac-2017-combinatorics-b-06.title: Set up the equation (official method)
pumac-2017-combinatorics-b-06.body:
Each copy behaves independently, and the whole family dies out iff every copy's family dies out. Conditioning on the first roll:
$$p=\frac14\left(1+p+p^2+p^3\right)\iff p^3+p^2-3p+1=0\iff(p-1)(p^2+2p-1)=0,$$
so $p\in\{1,\,-1\pm\sqrt2\}$. Negative values are impossible.

To rule out $p=1$: let $p_k$ be the probability that everything has vanished within $k$ rounds. Then $p_0=0$, $p_{k+1}=\frac14(1+p_k+p_k^2+p_k^3)$, and since the right side is increasing in $p_k$ and equals $\sqrt2-1$ at $p_k=\sqrt2-1$, induction gives $p_k<\sqrt2-1$ for all $k$. Hence $p=\lim p_k\le\sqrt2-1$, so $p=\sqrt2-1$.

Then $\frac{10}{p}=\frac{10}{\sqrt2-1}=10(\sqrt2+1)\approx24.14$, so the answer is $24$.

**Answer: 24**

pumac-2017-combinatorics-b-06.title: Branching-process theory
pumac-2017-combinatorics-b-06.body:
This is a Galton–Watson process with offspring mean $\frac{0+1+2+3}{4}=\frac32>1$, so the extinction probability is the **smallest** root in $[0,1]$ of $s=\frac14(1+s+s^2+s^3)$, which is $\sqrt2-1\approx0.4142$ (iterating $s\mapsto\frac14(1+s+s^2+s^3)$ from $0$ converges to it numerically). So $\left\lfloor\frac{10}{0.41421\ldots}\right\rfloor=\lfloor24.142\ldots\rfloor=24$.

**Answer: 24**

pumac-2017-combinatorics-b-07.title: Inversions and a product formula (official method)
pumac-2017-combinatorics-b-07.body:
By relabelling letters, the total cost does not depend on which target string is chosen, so take the target to be alphabetical order. The minimum number of adjacent swaps to sort a string is its number of **inversions** (pairs in the wrong order): each adjacent swap changes the inversion count by exactly $1$, and bubble sort achieves it.

So the cost is $\sum_{\sigma}2^{\operatorname{inv}(\sigma)}$ over the $120$ permutations. Build a permutation by inserting the letters in increasing order: when the $i$-th letter is inserted into a string of $i-1$ letters, it creates $0,1,\dots,i-1$ new inversions depending on the position (it is larger than all letters already there). Hence
$$\sum_\sigma 2^{\operatorname{inv}(\sigma)}=\prod_{i=1}^{5}\left(1+2+\dots+2^{i-1}\right)=\prod_{i=1}^5(2^i-1)=1\cdot3\cdot7\cdot15\cdot31=9765.$$

**Answer: 9765**

pumac-2017-combinatorics-b-07.title: Brute force check
pumac-2017-combinatorics-b-07.body:
A computer can try all $120$ targets: for each target and each of the $120$ permutations, count the inversions relative to the target and add $2^{\text{inv}}$. Every target gives the same total, $9765$, confirming the symmetry argument.

**Answer: 9765**

pumac-2017-combinatorics-b-08.title: Binomial identity (official method)
pumac-2017-combinatorics-b-08.body:
Let $p=\frac{17}{20}$ (stay) and $q=\frac3{20}$ (move). After $n$ steps, $d_n=1+k$ where $k\sim\text{Bin}(n,q)$. Using $\frac{1}{k+1}\binom nk=\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{n+1}{k+1}$:
$$E_n=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk\frac{q^kp^{n-k}}{k+1}=\frac{1}{q(n+1)}\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n+1}{k+1}q^{k+1}p^{n-k}=\frac{1-p^{n+1}}{q(n+1)}.$$
So $\frac1{E_n}=\frac{3(n+1)}{20\left(1-(17/20)^{n+1}\right)}$. For large $n$ the correction $(17/20)^{n+1}$ is astronomically small, so we need $\frac{3(n+1)}{20}>2017$ essentially, i.e. $n+1>\frac{40340}{3}=13446.67$, so $n+1\ge13447$.

Check: $n=13446$ gives $\frac{3\cdot13447}{20}=2017.05>2017$, while $n=13445$ gives $2016.9<2017$ (the tiny correction cannot bridge a gap of $0.1$).

**Answer: 13446**

pumac-2017-combinatorics-b-08.title: Integral representation
pumac-2017-combinatorics-b-08.body:
$\frac{1}{1+k}=\int_0^1 t^k\,dt$, so
$$E_n=\int_0^1E[t^k]\,dt=\int_0^1(p+qt)^n\,dt=\frac{(p+q)^{n+1}-p^{n+1}}{q(n+1)}=\frac{1-p^{n+1}}{q(n+1)},$$
the same formula. Exact rational evaluation confirms $\frac1{E_{13445}}\approx2016.90$ and $\frac1{E_{13446}}\approx2017.05$.

**Answer: 13446**
